questions.question: Two girls throw balls of about the same size at a wall, both at exactly the same speed. One throws a hollow plastic Wiffle ball with holes in one half; the other throws a tennis ball. Which ball carries more kinetic energy, and why?
questions.answer: The tennis ball, because it has more mass
choices: The tennis ball, because it has more mass
The tennis ball, because it is bouncier
Both the same, because their speeds are equal
Both the same, because their sizes are equal
questions.context: Kinetic energy depends on an object's mass as well as its speed. At the same speed, the tennis ball has about three times the Wiffle ball's mass and so carries about three times the kinetic energy, which is why it stings far more when it hits. How bouncy or how big a ball is does not change its kinetic energy.
questions.grade_note: The middle-school standard NGSS MS-PS3-1 uses this very case, a Wiffle ball against a tennis ball, to teach that kinetic energy grows with mass at the same speed.

questions.question: A cyclist on a flat road pedals harder until she is going twice as fast as before. Her mass and the bike's stay the same. What happens to her kinetic energy?
questions.answer: It becomes four times as great
choices: It becomes four times as great
It becomes twice as great
It becomes eight times as great
It stays the same, since energy cannot be created
questions.context: Kinetic energy grows with the square of speed: twice as fast means four times the kinetic energy, while twice the mass would mean only twice as much. The extra energy is not made from nothing; her legs turn the chemical energy from her food into the motion of the bike.
questions.grade_note: NGSS MS-PS3-1's core idea is that kinetic energy is proportional to mass and grows with the square of speed, taught as a relationship without calculation; 'it doubles' is the recorded mistake.

questions.question: A girl carries her backpack up the stairs from the ground floor to the third floor of her school and sets it on a desk. Compared with when it lay on the ground floor, what is true of the backpack's gravitational potential energy?
questions.answer: It is greater, because the pack is higher up
choices: It is greater, because the pack is higher up
It is less, because she spent energy lifting it
It is the same, because its mass has not changed
It is zero, because the pack is sitting still
questions.context: Gravitational potential energy is stored energy that grows the higher an object is lifted. Carrying the pack upstairs took energy from the girl's food, and some of it is now stored in the pack's height. A pack sitting still can still hold energy, ready to change into motion if it falls.
questions.grade_note: Texas's grade 6 standard TEKS 6.8A names gravitational potential energy, and NGSS MS-PS3-2 compares objects at different heights.

questions.question: An archer pulls her bowstring back to her cheek and holds it there while she aims. The bow's limbs bend as the string pulls tight. In what form does the bent bow store the energy that will send the arrow flying?
choices: Elastic potential energy
Gravitational potential energy
Chemical potential energy
Kinetic energy
questions.context: Bending the bow's limbs stores elastic potential energy, the same kind a stretched rubber band or a squeezed spring holds. When she lets go, the limbs spring back and the stored energy becomes the arrow's kinetic energy. Her muscles' chemical energy did the bending, but the bend itself now holds the energy.
questions.grade_note: TEKS 6.8A names elastic potential energy beside gravitational and chemical, and the drawn bow is a standard example of it.

questions.question: Gasoline in a car's tank, a granola bar in a backpack and a new battery in a drawer each hold a store of energy. While they just sit there, none of it comes out. What has to happen to release it?
questions.answer: They must react and become new substances
choices: They must react and become new substances
They must be lifted up high and then dropped
They must be squeezed or stretched out of shape
They must be set moving very fast
questions.context: All three hold chemical potential energy, stored in the way their atoms are joined, and it comes out only in a chemical reaction that makes new substances. Gasoline burns in the engine, the body breaks down the bar's sugars in its cells, and the chemicals inside the battery react when it is put to work in a circuit. Lifting, squeezing or speeding them up would store or carry other kinds of energy, not this one.
questions.grade_note: TEKS 6.8A names chemical potential energy, stored in food, fuel and batteries; 6th grade adds that a chemical reaction releases it.

questions.question: A motor-driven chain hauls a roller coaster train slowly up its first hill. At the top the train tips over and plunges down the far side, faster and faster. What energy change makes it speed up as it drops?
questions.answer: Gravitational potential energy changes into kinetic energy
choices: Gravitational potential energy changes into kinetic energy
Kinetic energy changes into gravitational potential energy
Electrical energy from the motor changes into kinetic energy
Gravity makes brand new kinetic energy as it falls
questions.context: At the top of the hill the train holds the most gravitational potential energy, because it is highest. As it drops, that stored energy changes into kinetic energy, so it goes faster the lower it gets. The motor's energy went into lifting the train, nothing pushes it on the drop, and gravity makes no new energy: the train trades height for speed, and on the next climb trades speed back for height.
questions.grade_note: TEKS 6.8B teaches energy conserved in amusement park rides, and NGSS MS-PS3-2 uses a roller coaster cart at different places on a hill.

questions.question: A physics teacher hangs a heavy bowling ball from the ceiling on a long rope. With his head against a wall, he holds the ball to his nose and lets go without a push. It swings away and back, and stops just short of his face. What makes him sure it cannot hit him?
questions.answer: It cannot gain more energy than it began with
choices: It cannot gain more energy than it began with
Gravity pulls harder on it as it swings back
A heavy ball slows more than a light one
Its energy is destroyed a little each swing
questions.context: Energy is never created or destroyed. Let go without a push, the ball starts with a fixed amount of energy, stored by its height, so at the end of each swing it can climb back only as high as his nose and no higher. A push would add energy, and then it could hit him; a little energy turns into heat in the air and at the hook on every swing, so the ball comes back just short.
questions.grade_note: Energy that is never created or destroyed is grade 6 content (Texas's older TEKS 6 wording names the law), and the bowling-ball pendulum is the classic demonstration of it.

questions.question: A girl on a playground swing stops pumping her legs. Each swing is a little lower than the one before, until at last she hangs still. What has become of the energy of her swinging?
questions.answer: Friction and the air changed it into heat
choices: Friction and the air changed it into heat
It was used up, and now it no longer exists
It is stored as potential energy in the swing
It went back into her body as chemical energy
questions.context: Rubbing at the swing's hooks and pushing through the air turn a little of her energy into heat (thermal energy) on every swing, until none of the motion is left. The warmth is spread so thin that no one can feel it, but the energy still exists. Hanging still at the bottom, she holds less potential energy than at the top of a swing, not more.
questions.grade_note: The grade 6 conservation unit teaches that friction turns some motion into heat, and that energy is not used up; 'used up' is the recorded mistake.

questions.question: In a game of pool, a player strikes the cue ball hard and straight into a still ball, hitting it head on. The cue ball stops almost dead on the spot. Where has most of its kinetic energy gone?
questions.answer: Into the ball that it struck
choices: Into the ball that it struck
Into the sound of the click
Into heat in the table's cloth
Into energy stored in the cue ball
questions.context: When one object strikes another, energy can pass from one to the other. Here the cue ball's kinetic energy passes to the ball it hits, which rolls off almost as fast as the cue ball was going. Only a little becomes the click's sound and heat, and the stopped cue ball keeps nothing stored up.
questions.grade_note: NGSS MS-PS3-5 teaches that when an object's kinetic energy changes, energy is passed to or from it, and the cue ball is the textbook case.
